{{Short description|Integral transform used in various branches of mathematics}}
{{For|summation transformation|summation by parts}}
In [[mathematics]], the '''Abel transform''',<ref>{{cite journal|first=N. H. |last=Abel |journal=[[Crelle's Journal|Journal für die reine und angewandte Mathematik]] |volume=1 |pages=153–157 |date=1826|title=Auflösung einer mechanischen Aufgabe|doi=10.1515/crll.1826.1.153|url=https://eudml.org/doc/183021|language=de}}</ref> named for [[Niels Henrik Abel]], is an [[integral transform]] often used in the analysis of spherically symmetric or axially symmetric functions. The Abel transform of a function {{math|''f''(''r'')}} is given by

: <math>F(y) = 2 \int_y^\infty \frac{f(r)r}{\sqrt{r^2 - y^2}} \,dr.</math>

Assuming that {{math|''f''(''r'')}} drops to zero more quickly than {{math|{{sfrac|1|''r''}}}}, the inverse Abel transform is given by

: <math>f(r) = -\frac{1}{\pi} \int_r^\infty \frac{dF}{dy} \,\frac{dy}{\sqrt{y^2 - r^2}}.</math>

In [[image analysis]], the forward Abel transform is used to project an optically thin, axially symmetric emission function onto a plane, and the inverse Abel transform is used to calculate the emission function given a projection (i.e. a scan or a photograph) of that emission function.

In [[absorption spectroscopy]] of cylindrical flames or plumes, the forward Abel transform is the integrated [[absorbance]] along a ray with closest distance {{mvar|y}} from the center of the flame, while the inverse Abel transform gives the local [[absorption coefficient]] at a distance {{mvar|r}} from the center. Abel transform is limited to applications with axially symmetric geometries. For more general asymmetrical cases, more general-oriented reconstruction algorithms such as [[algebraic reconstruction technique]] (ART), maximum likelihood expectation maximization (MLEM), filtered back-projection (FBP) algorithms should be employed.

In recent years, the inverse Abel transform (and its variants) has become the cornerstone of data analysis in [[photofragment-ion imaging]] and [[Photofragment-ion imaging#Electron imaging|photoelectron imaging]]. Among recent most notable extensions of inverse Abel transform are the "onion peeling" and "basis set expansion" (BASEX) methods of photoelectron and photoion image analysis.

== Geometrical interpretation ==

[[File:AbelTransform.png|thumb|right|256px|A geometrical interpretation of the Abel transform in two dimensions. An observer ({{math|I}}) looks along a line parallel to the {{mvar|x}} axis a distance {{mvar|y}} above the origin. What the observer sees is the projection (i.e. the integral) of the circularly symmetric function {{math|''f''(''r'')}} along the line of sight. The function {{math|''f''(''r'')}} is represented in gray in this figure. The observer is assumed to be located infinitely far from the origin so that the limits of integration are {{math|±∞}}.]]

In two dimensions, the Abel transform {{math|''F''(''y'')}} can be interpreted as the projection of a circularly symmetric function {{math|''f''(''r'')}} along a set of parallel lines of sight at a distance {{mvar|y}} from the origin. Referring to the figure on the right, the observer ({{math|I}}) will see

: <math>F(y) = \int_{-\infty}^\infty f\left(\sqrt{x^2 + y^2}\right) \,dx,</math>

where {{math|''f''(''r'')}} is the circularly [[symmetric function]] represented by the gray color in the figure. It is assumed that the observer is actually at {{math|''x'' {{=}} ∞}}, so that the limits of integration are {{math|±∞}}, and all lines of sight are parallel to the {{mvar|x}} axis. Realizing that the [[radius]] {{mvar|r}} is related to {{mvar|x}} and {{mvar|y}} as {{math|''r''<sup>2</sup> {{=}} ''x''<sup>2</sup> + ''y''<sup>2</sup>}}, it follows that

: <math>dx = \frac{r\,dr}{\sqrt{r^2 - y^2}}</math>

for {{math|''x'' > 0}}. Since {{math|''f''(''r'')}} is an [[even function]] in {{mvar|x}}, we may write

: <math>
F(y) = 2 \int_0^\infty f\left(\sqrt{x^2 + y^2}\right) \,dx =  2 \int_{|y|}^\infty f(r)\,\frac{r\,dr}{\sqrt{r^2 - y^2}},
</math>

which yields the Abel transform of {{math|''f''(''r'')}}.

The Abel transform may be extended to higher dimensions. Of particular interest is the extension to three dimensions. If we have an axially symmetric function {{math|''f''(''ρ'', ''z'')}}, where {{math|''ρ''<sup>2</sup> {{=}} ''x''<sup>2</sup> + ''y''<sup>2</sup>}} is the cylindrical radius, then we may want to know the projection of that function onto a plane parallel to the ''z'' axis. [[Without loss of generality]], we can take that plane to be the {{mvar|yz}} plane, so that

: <math> F(y, z) = \int_{-\infty}^\infty f(\rho, z) \,dx = 2 \int_y^\infty \frac{f(\rho, z) \rho \,d\rho}{\sqrt{\rho^2 - y^2}}, </math>

which is just the Abel transform of {{math|''f''(''ρ'', ''z'')}} in {{mvar|ρ}} and {{mvar|y}}.

A particular type of [[axial symmetry]] is spherical symmetry. In this case, we have a function {{math|''f''(''r'')}}, where {{math|''r''<sup>2</sup> {{=}} ''x''<sup>2</sup> + ''y''<sup>2</sup> + ''z''<sup>2</sup>}}. The projection onto, say, the {{mvar|yz}} plane will then be circularly symmetric and expressible as {{math|''F''(''s'')}}, where {{math|''s''<sup>2</sup> {{=}} ''y''<sup>2</sup> + ''z''<sup>2</sup>}}. Carrying out the integration, we have

: <math> F(s) = \int_{-\infty}^\infty f(r) \,dx = 2 \int_s^\infty \frac{f(r) r \,dr}{\sqrt{r^2 - s^2}},</math>

which is again, the Abel transform of {{math|''f''(''r'')}} in {{mvar|r}} and {{mvar|s}}.

== Verification of the inverse Abel transform ==
Assuming {{mvar|f}} is continuously differentiable, and {{mvar|f}}, {{mvar|f′}} drop to zero faster than {{math|{{sfrac|1|''r''}}}}, we can integrate by parts by setting
:<math>u=f(r) ,\quad v' = \frac{r}\sqrt{r^2-y^2}, </math>
to find
:<math>F(y) = -2 \int_y^\infty f'(r) \sqrt{r^2-y^2} \, dr.</math>

Differentiating [[Differentiation under the integral sign|formally]],

:<math>F'(y) = 2 y \int_y^\infty \frac{f'(r)}{\sqrt{r^2-y^2}} \, dr.</math>

Now substitute this into the inverse Abel transform formula:

:<math>-\frac{1}{\pi} \int_r^\infty \frac{F'(y)}{\sqrt{y^2-r^2}} \, dy = \int_r^\infty \int_y^\infty \frac{-2 y}{\pi \sqrt{\left(y^2-r^2\right) \left(s^2-y^2\right)}} f'(s) \, ds dy.</math>

By [[Fubini's theorem]], the last integral equals

:<math>\int_r^\infty \int_r^s \frac{-2 y}{\pi \sqrt{\left(y^2-r^2\right) \left(s^2-y^2\right)}} \, dy f'(s) \,ds = \int_r^\infty (-1) f'(s) \, ds = f(r).</math>

== Generalization of the Abel transform to discontinuous {{math|''F''(''y'')}} ==

Consider the case where {{math|''F''(''y'')}} is discontinuous at {{math|''y'' {{=}} ''y''<sub>Δ</sub>}}, where it abruptly changes its value by a finite amount {{math|Δ''F''}}. That is, {{math|''y''<sub>Δ</sub>}} and {{math|Δ''F''}} are defined by
:<math>\Delta F \equiv \lim_{\varepsilon\rightarrow 0} \bigl( F(y_\Delta-\varepsilon) - F(y_\Delta+\varepsilon) \bigr).</math>

Such a situation is encountered in tethered polymers ([[Polymer brush]]) exhibiting a vertical [[phase separation]], where {{math|''F''(''y'')}} stands for the polymer density profile and <math>f(r)</math> is related to the spatial distribution of terminal, non-tethered monomers of the polymers.

The Abel transform of a function {{math|''f''(''r'')}} is under these circumstances again given by:

:<math>F(y)=2\int_y^\infty \frac{f(r)r\,dr}{\sqrt{r^2-y^2}}.</math>

Assuming {{math|''f''(''r'')}} drops to zero more quickly than {{math|{{sfrac|1|''r''}}}}, the inverse Abel transform is however given by

:<math>
f(r)=\left( \frac{1}{2}\delta\left(r-y_\Delta\right)\sqrt{1-\left(\frac{y_\Delta}{r}\right)^2} - \frac{1}{\pi} \frac{H\left(y_\Delta-r\right)}{\sqrt{y_\Delta^2-r^2}} \right) \Delta F-\frac{1}{\pi}\int_r^\infty\frac{d F}{dy}\frac{dy}{\sqrt{y^2-r^2}}.
</math>

where {{mvar|δ}} is the [[Dirac delta function]] and {{math|''H''(''x'')}} the [[Heaviside step function]]. The extended version of the Abel transform for discontinuous {{mvar|F}} is proven upon applying the Abel transform to shifted, continuous {{math|''F''(''y'')}}, and it reduces to the classical Abel transform when {{math|Δ''F'' {{=}} 0}}. If {{math|''F''(''y'')}} has more than a single discontinuity, one has to introduce shifts for any of them to come up with a generalized version of the inverse Abel transform which contains {{mvar|n}} additional terms, each of them corresponding to one of the {{mvar|n}} discontinuities.

== Relationship to other integral transforms ==

=== Relationship to the Fourier and Hankel transforms ===
The Abel transform is one member of the [[Projection-slice theorem|FHA cycle]] of integral operators. For example, in two dimensions, if we define {{mvar|A}} as the Abel transform operator, {{mvar|F}} as the [[Fourier transform]] operator and {{mvar|H}} as the zeroth-order [[Hankel transform]] operator, then the special case of the [[projection-slice theorem]] for circularly symmetric functions states that

: <math>FA = H.</math>

In other words, applying the Abel transform to a one-dimensional function and then applying the Fourier transform to that result is the same as applying the Hankel transform to that function. This concept can be extended to higher dimensions.

=== Relationship to the Radon transform ===

Abel transform can be viewed as the [[Radon transform]] of an isotropic 2D function {{math|''f''(''r'')}}. As {{math|''f''(''r'')}} is isotropic, its Radon transform is the same at different angles of the viewing axis. Thus, the Abel transform is a function of the distance along the viewing axis only.
